author: Abdellah Taïa
en_title: Le Bastion des larmes: There Is No Paperwork for Leaving a Family
zh_title: 《泪之堡垒》：他回乡卖掉母亲的房子，却不能只谈房子
en_deck: Youssef returns to Salé to sell his mother’s apartment. His sisters, his first love, and his own unfinished anger will not fit neatly into a transaction.
zh_deck: 母亲去世十年后，Youssef想尽快卖房离开。但姐姐们有她们的生活，过去也有尚未说完的话。
en_notice: Introduces the reason for Youssef’s return and the opening relationships, without revealing later encounters or the ending. The novel includes homophobia, family trauma, sexual violence, and abuse of minors; this guide does not describe the violence. The French title is retained here. Emma Ramadan lists an English translation for 2027, without a confirmed English title.
zh_notice: 介绍返乡缘由与开篇关系，不描述暴力细节，不交代后段相遇和结局。作品涉及同性情感、家庭创伤、性暴力与权力压迫，包括未成年人受侵害的内容。《泪之堡垒》为本文暂译；英译者Emma Ramadan列有2027年出版计划，尚未确认正式英文书名，英文页面保留法文原标题。
en_body:
Youssef has a practical reason to go back to Morocco. His mother has been dead for ten years. His sisters want her apartment sold. He will return to Salé, deal with the property, and get back to his life in France.

It sounds like a journey that can be given a return date. Complete the transaction and the remaining connection becomes somebody else’s address.

Abdellah Taïa’s *Le Bastion des larmes* does not begin with the paperwork. It takes us back to the mother’s death, when Youssef’s six older sisters decide to clear her debts within three days. He offers to contribute. They refuse. This is something the daughters will do.

Before the returning son can occupy the center of the story, the sisters have made their own decision. The family is not waiting, motionless, for him to come home and explain it.

## The sisters were already doing something

The [French opening published by Julliard](https://www.calameo.com/books/0069907784ab1ca439055) gives this refusal a wonderfully unsettling simplicity. The sisters invoke a tradition. Youssef has never heard of it. Something he does not know is happening among the people he thinks he knows.

We need not turn their statement into a rule about Moroccan families. It matters here as a claim made by these women, in this family, at this moment. They have identified an obligation and taken possession of it.

Bereavement consequently arrives as more than a private feeling. Someone has to deal with what the dead person has left behind. Doing so can establish a new arrangement among the living, one that does not require every relative to agree or participate.

By the time of Youssef’s return ten years later, the apartment remains, but the family once gathered around its mother has changed. Calling someone a sister does not settle how to speak to her now. A shared childhood provides material for a relationship; it cannot conduct that relationship on the siblings’ behalf.

In an [interview with L’Éclaireur Fnac](https://leclaireur.fnac.com/article/545202-abdellah-taia-pour-le-bastion-des-larmes-la-litteraritesrature-est-une-maniere-de-tendre-la-main-aux-autres/), Taïa describes a question that helped set the novel in motion: after parents die, what will continue to hold their children together? His own experience informs the question, though Youssef should not be treated as a documentary transcript of the author.

You do not have to share the character’s history to recognize the difficulty. For years, going home may have meant visiting a parent. Once that reason disappears, seeing a sibling becomes a choice that needs reasons of its own. Nobody has ceased to matter. The old arrangements simply no longer do all the work.

## The person who left does not know everything

A teacher who has lived in France for twenty-five years might seem to have escaped the life his sisters remained inside. That is an easy story to tell from a distance. It sorts the family into freedom on one side and confinement on the other.

The novel’s starting relationships resist such a clean distribution. Leaving can transform a life without making it enviable in every respect. Staying does not turn a person into a figure whose only remaining task is to wait to be understood.

In the Fnac conversation, Taïa recalls a mutual misreading. Relatives at home could regard France as proof of success, while the person abroad might imagine that those who stayed had plentiful companionship and love. Each position could invent advantages in the other.

There is an everyday cruelty in that mistake. Once I am certain that you have what I lack, your difficulty can sound like ingratitude. Why are you unhappy when you have already been given so much? Both people may be asking versions of that question, leaving neither able to describe a life the other would recognize.

But the hurts in *Le Bastion des larmes* are not reducible to failures of communication. Youssef’s past includes violence directed at him as a gay boy and failures of protection within relationships that should have offered safety. A vague acknowledgment that everyone has suffered would be an inadequate response.

That is why his continuing attachment is interesting. In [his Benzine review](https://www.benzinemag.net/2024/10/23/le-bastion-des-larmes-dabdellah-taia-les-souffrances-du-jeune-youssef/), Jean-François Lahorgue notices the force of rage and resentment alongside the possibility of forgiveness. The tension offers a way into Youssef without prescribing what he ought to do.

Wanting to be close to family need not mean that the anger has passed. Remembering harm need not empty every other memory of meaning. A person may find those feelings hard to hold together precisely because both are real.

The reader’s temptation is to tidy them up: forgive, or cut ties; return, or finally leave. Either instruction would spare us some uncertainty. It would also replace Youssef’s wishes with our preferred account of a good decision.

He is allowed to want something more complicated than an observer’s solution. Whether he can speak to his sisters differently, and what they might have to say to him, are questions for the unfolding novel.

## A voice arrives before the journey

Najib belongs to Youssef’s younger life and his experience of love. Yet he does not wait in the narrative as background to be explained after the return. He is already appearing in Youssef’s dreams before the trip.

An [English excerpt in The Markaz Review](https://themarkaz.org/return-to-sale-an-excerpt-from-le-bastion-des-larmes/) offers a direct encounter with this voice. The dream calls Youssef back into a relationship rather than merely supplying information about one. A remembered person has things to say; the man doing the remembering does not control every term of the conversation.

In the French sample, short sentences, repetitions, and direct address make the past feel insistently present. The language can be straightforward while the feeling it carries is anything but settled. A thought comes back because its pressure has not been relieved by being stated once.

Taïa gives a striking account of this rhythm in his [Diacritik interview with Jean-Philippe Cazier](https://diacritik.com/2024/08/27/abdellah-taia-il-faut-se-revolter-sans-lautorisation-du-pouvoir-le-bastion-des-larmes/). He traces his writing to the speech of his mother and sisters: their repeated returns to events, their arguments, and their determination to tell their own versions.

The observation makes literary influence something we can hear. It is not simply that a writer has family members who inspired characters. Their ways of going over an experience can enter the pace of a sentence. What sounds repetitive to somebody listening from outside may be the speaker’s unfinished attempt to get an experience said.

For a reader accustomed to an even, explanatory narrator, this proximity can be demanding. The sentences do not always provide the comfortable space in which to consider strong feelings at leisure.

Lahorgue’s review includes a useful reservation: poetic softness can sometimes, in his view, lessen the impact of the violence being represented. That is not a verdict we have to adopt in advance. It is a question worth noticing as we read. Does the language make room for tenderness without smoothing away the injury that makes tenderness difficult?

## What selling can finish

This is not a book for every mood. Its subject matter can be painful, and there is no obligation to prove one’s seriousness by reading material one needs to avoid.

Its invitation is nevertheless more open than a story about finding roots, or confirming that escape was right. Youssef has a past he cannot simply cancel, and a future he still has to decide how to live. Neither belongs entirely to those who hurt him or those who think they know what would be best for him.

The apartment can pass to another owner. A sale has procedures, signatures, and a point at which it is complete. A relationship has no comparable document.

Youssef would like this journey to finish something. The novel gives us good reason to wonder what, exactly, finishing would mean.
zh_body:
母亲去世十年以后，Youssef应姐妹们的要求回萨累处理房产。他在法国当教师，已经生活了二十五年；这次只想尽快卖掉房子，然后回去。

如果只从手续上说，这是一趟可以安排归期的旅行。房子卖完，事情办妥，一个人就能够回到自己现在的生活里。

但Abdellah Taïa的《泪之堡垒》并没有从签字、议价或者收拾旧物开始。它先把读者带回母亲刚去世的时候：六个姐姐决定在三天内还清母亲的债。Youssef提出帮忙，被拒绝了。她们说，这是女儿们的事。

在一部由返乡展开的小说里，读者首先看见的，不是一个安静等着主人公回来解释的家庭，而是已经作出决定、正在行动的姐姐们。

## 母亲走了，姐妹们仍然有自己的事情要做

[Julliard公开的法文开篇](https://www.calameo.com/books/0069907784ab1ca439055)里，姐姐们说这是传统，Youssef却从未听过。他不熟悉的事情，已经在他熟悉的家中展开。她们这样解释自己的决定，并不需要被我们扩写成所有摩洛哥家庭都遵循的一条规则。

还债让“失去母亲”不只是一个人的内心感受。家里原本依靠她维持的秩序突然空了，活着的人需要决定，接下来怎样承担她留下来的东西。

这个位置，比一个归乡者站在家庭中央、重新发现所有人的安排更有张力。他不是唯一离开旧日生活的人，也不是唯一经历失去的人。家人可以很重要，同时又不围着他的感受展开。

到了十年后的这次返乡，房子仍然在，围绕母亲形成的家庭却已经变了。每个人都在过自己的日子，兄弟姐妹的称呼没有消失，称呼背后还能怎样相处，却不再是一件理所当然的事。

Taïa在接受[L’Éclaireur Fnac访谈](https://leclaireur.fnac.com/article/545202-abdellah-taia-pour-le-bastion-des-larmes-la-litteraritesrature-est-une-maniere-de-tendre-la-main-aux-autres/)时，谈到一个推动写作的问题：父母不在以后，兄弟姐妹之间的联系依靠什么继续？他由自己的经历进入这个问题，但小说里的Youssef不是作者生平的一份逐项记录。

对于有相似经验的读者，这可能比“如何回到故乡”更贴近生活。父母在的时候，回家有一个清楚的目的；此后，要不要联系、为什么见面，常常需要重新寻找理由。共同的过去不会凭空消失，却也未必足够替现在的相处作安排。

## 离开的人，并不掌握唯一真实的故事

Youssef在法国生活，而姐姐们留在摩洛哥。只看这个差别，很容易把他们想成分处自由与束缚两端的人：他已经走出去了，她们还被留在原处。

这样的想象不够用。远行可能改变一个人的处境，却不会保证他从此获得一种人人向往的生活；留下来的人，也不会因为没有离开，就只剩下等待被理解的命运。

Taïa在同一访谈中，谈到彼此羡慕背后的误认：留在故乡的家人容易把法国看成成功的证明，远行者又容易想象，留在家中的人拥有更多相伴与爱。作者所说的是自己的经验，也为小说中的隔阂提供了一个入口。

有时候，怨气并不来自完全不关心，而是来自一种过分肯定的想象：既然你已经过得那么好了，为什么还不能理解我？当双方都这样想，谁也很难把自己的困难说出口。

不过，《泪之堡垒》里的距离，不只是几年没有认真聊天而已。Youssef早年作为同性恋者承受过伤害，那些本应保护他的亲近关系，也留下了深刻的缺口。回乡使这些事情重新进入眼前，不能靠“大家都不容易”便一笔带过。

Jean-François Lahorgue在[Benzine的评论](https://www.benzinemag.net/2024/10/23/le-bastion-des-larmes-dabdellah-taia-les-souffrances-du-jeune-youssef/)中，注意到小说中的愤怒、怨恨与原谅的可能。由此再看Youssef，便会发现：一个人想靠近家人，并不表示他已经不再怨恨；他记得伤害，也不表示除此之外，再没有别的记忆。

这种写法值得保留它的不整齐。若我们急着决定Youssef应该原谅，或应该彻底断绝关系，就会把他重新变成一套处事原则的执行者。更难也更动人的部分，是让他仍然能够有自己的愿望，而这些愿望不必与旁观者认定的最佳选择一致。

他会怎样面对姐姐们，又能从她们那里听到怎样的回应，需要继续读下去才知道。这里的吸引力不是等待一项秘密使所有误会消失，而是那些有过共同生活的人，是否还可能说出没有被旧身份规定好的话。

## 过去不是背景，它会开口叫他的名字

返乡的故事还牵连着Najib。那是Youssef年轻时爱过的人，也是理解他的过去时无法绕开的人物。出发以前，Najib已经在他的梦里出现。

从公开试读看，这些声音的进入不依赖复杂的词语。短句、重复和直接的呼唤很明显。某个念头不是被解释一次就放下，而是重新回来，带着还没有平复的情绪。[The Markaz Review刊载的英译节选](https://themarkaz.org/return-to-sale-an-excerpt-from-le-bastion-des-larmes/)也可以让英语读者直接接近这段梦中的声音；它是单独刊出的节选，不是尚待出版的完整英译本。

Taïa在接受[Diacritik访谈](https://diacritik.com/2024/08/27/abdellah-taia-il-faut-se-revolter-sans-lautorisation-du-pouvoir-le-bastion-des-larmes/)时，把自己写作的节奏追溯到母亲与姐姐们说话的方式。她们反复谈论经历过的事情，争辩、拆解，试着说出自己的版本。他的法语写作也在寻找一种能够容纳那些声音的形式。

这使“家人影响了他的写作”不只是一项背景资料。影响可以具体到一句话怎样回来、同一件事为什么不能讲一遍就结束。对于讲述者，旁人已经听懂了，并不等于自己终于把它说完了。

若习惯了从容的旁白，这种贴近呼喊与诉说的节奏可能会显得强烈。它并不总给人留下一段舒适的旁观距离。句子容易进入，情绪却未必轻省。

Lahorgue的评论在肯定小说力量的同时，也认为某些段落的诗意过于柔和，可能减弱所写暴力的冲击。这份保留提示了一个值得留意的问题：当一种语言试着同时承受爱与伤害时，读者是否会觉得，它对两者都足够诚实？

所以，这不是适合任何时刻翻开的书。正在避开相关创伤题材的读者，可以不急着读它；愿意进入这段故事，也不需要把承受最难的部分当成一种道德考验。

它值得被介绍，是因为返乡在这里不只等于寻找根，也不只等于确认自己当年离开得对。Youssef有一段不能简单取消的过去，同时仍然是一个需要决定接下来怎样生活的人。

房子可以作为遗产处理，关系却没有同样明确的交接手续。卖掉它，能不能使Youssef更自由？再见到那些人，又会不会让自由变成一个不同的问题？《泪之堡垒》从这些尚未谈妥的事情里，继续向前。
en_source_note: Close observations follow Julliard’s French opening; The Markaz Review separately publishes an English excerpt. Taïa’s Fnac and Diacritik interviews provide context about siblings, exile, and spoken rhythms, while Lahorgue’s review supplies an explicitly attributed reservation. The date is the original French publication. Emma Ramadan’s translation list records a 2027 English edition under the French title; the Chinese title here is a working translation.
zh_source_note: 具体场景依Julliard法文开篇；The Markaz Review另有单独刊出的英译节选。Fnac与Diacritik作者访谈补充兄弟姐妹、离乡与口语节奏的背景，Lahorgue书评提供明确署名的阅读保留。出版日期为法文原作首版日期；Emma Ramadan的翻译书目以法文原标题列有2027年英译计划，中文标题为本文暂译。
